title: UNIT 5: SIMPLE MACHINES
notes:
✓ Simple machine → Device that makes mechanical work easier by changing the magnitude or direction of a force or the distance through which it acts.

✓ Simple machines → Do not create energy; they transfer mechanical energy.

◆ SIX TYPES
✓ Inclined plane.
✓ Wedge.
✓ Screw.
✓ Lever.
✓ Wheel and axle.
✓ Pulley.

title: 5.1 SIMPLE MACHINES AND THEIR PURPOSES
notes:
✓ Simple machines → Make work easier by changing the direction of force, multiplying force, or multiplying speed or distance.

◆ PURPOSES
✓ Changing the direction of force.
✓ Multiplying force.
✓ Multiplying speed or distance.

✓ Effort → Force applied to a machine.
✓ Load → Force exerted by the machine on the object being moved.

✓ Work input = Effort × distance moved by effort.

✓ Work output = Load × distance moved by load.

title: 5.2 SIMPLE MACHINES AT HOME
notes:
✓ Simple machines → Are commonly found in everyday household activities.

◆ EXAMPLES
✓ Knife → Wedge → Cutting.
✓ Bottle opener → Lever → Multiplies force.
✓ Screw → Holds objects together.
✓ Pulley → Changes direction or reduces effort.
✓ Wheel and axle → Transfers or multiplies force.

✓ Simple machines → Are the basic building blocks of many complex machines.

title: 5.3 SIMPLE MACHINES AT WORKPLACE
notes:
✓ Simple machines → Are used in workplaces to make lifting, cutting, carrying and moving objects easier.

◆ CLASSIFICATION BY PURPOSE
✓ Force multipliers → Increase output force.
✓ Speed/distance multipliers → Increase output distance or speed.
✓ Direction changers → Change the direction of the applied force.

title: 5.4 CLASSIFICATION OF SIMPLE MACHINES
notes:
✓ Simple machines → Are classified into two groups.

◆ INCLINED PLANES
✓ Inclined plane/ramp.
✓ Wedge.
✓ Screw.

◆ LEVERS
✓ Lever.
✓ Wheel and axle.
✓ Pulley.

✓ Compound machine → Combination of two or more simple machines.

✓ Examples → Bicycle, wire cutter and car.

title: 5.4.1 FORCE, SPEED AND DIRECTION MULTIPLIERS
notes:
✓ Force multiplier → Load > effort; a smaller effort lifts a larger load.

✓ Speed/distance multiplier → Load moves a greater distance than the effort in the same time.

✓ Direction changer → Changes the direction in which the load moves compared with the effort.

✓ Machine → Cannot multiply energy; it only transfers mechanical energy.

title: 5.5 MECHANICAL ADVANTAGE, VELOCITY RATIO AND EFFICIENCY
notes:
✓ Mechanical Advantage (M.A) → Ratio of output force to input force.

M.A = Load / Effort

✓ Velocity Ratio (V.R) → Ratio of distance moved by effort to distance moved by load.

V.R = Distance moved by effort / Distance moved by load

✓ Efficiency (η) → Ratio of work output to work input.

η = M.A / V.R × 100%

✓ Real machines → Lose energy mainly through friction, so efficiency is less than 100%.

title: 5.5.1 LEVERS
notes:
✓ Lever → Rigid bar that turns about a fixed point called the fulcrum.

◆ PARTS OF A LEVER
✓ Fulcrum → Pivot point.
✓ Load arm → Distance from fulcrum to load.
✓ Effort arm → Distance from fulcrum to effort.

✓ M.A = Load / Effort.
✓ V.R = Effort arm / Load arm.

title: 5.5.2 THREE CLASSES OF LEVERS
notes:
◆ FIRST-CLASS LEVER
✓ Fulcrum → Lies between effort and load.
✓ Examples → Seesaw, scissors, crowbar.
✓ M.A → Can be >, = or < 1.

◆ SECOND-CLASS LEVER
✓ Load → Lies between fulcrum and effort.
✓ Examples → Wheelbarrow, bottle opener, nutcracker.
✓ M.A → > 1.

◆ THIRD-CLASS LEVER
✓ Effort → Lies between fulcrum and load.
✓ Examples → Fishing rod, tweezers, broom, human arm.
✓ M.A → < 1.

title: 5.5.3 INCLINED PLANE
notes:
✓ Inclined plane → Sloping surface used to raise or lower a load with less effort.

✓ M.A = Load / Effort.

✓ V.R = Length of slope / Height of slope.

V.R = l / h

✓ Longer slope → Requires less effort, but the load moves through a greater distance.

title: 5.5.4 WEDGE
notes:
✓ Wedge → Device made from inclined planes and used to split or separate objects.

✓ Examples → Knife, axe, nail and spear.

✓ M.A = Load / Effort.

✓ V.R = Penetration length / Wedge thickness.

V.R = l / t

✓ Efficiency = M.A / V.R × 100%.

title: 5.5.5 SCREW
notes:
✓ Screw → Cylinder with a helical thread around it.

✓ Uses → Joining objects, digging and boring.

✓ Pitch (p) → Distance between successive threads.

✓ Screw → Converts rotational motion into linear motion.

◆ IDEAL MECHANICAL ADVANTAGE
IMA = πd / p

d → Average diameter of screw.
p → Pitch.

title: 5.5.6 WHEEL AND AXLE
notes:
✓ Wheel and axle → Wheel attached to a smaller axle so that both rotate together.

✓ M.A = Load / Effort.

✓ V.R = Radius of wheel / Radius of axle.

V.R = R / r

✓ Examples → Bicycle, car tire, screwdriver, drill, windmill and doorknob.

✓ Wheel and axle → Depending on where the effort is applied, it can act as a force or speed multiplier.

title: 5.5.7 PULLEY SYSTEM
notes:
✓ Pulley → Grooved wheel that rotates about its center and carries a rope or cable.

◆ TYPES OF PULLEYS
✓ Fixed pulley → Mainly changes the direction of force.
✓ Movable pulley → Reduces the effort required; ideal V.R = 2.
✓ Compound pulley → Combination of fixed and movable pulleys; also called block and tackle.

✓ M.A = Load / Effort.
✓ V.R = Number of rope sections supporting the load.

title: 5.5.8 WORK INPUT, WORK OUTPUT AND EFFICIENCY
notes:
✓ Work input = Effort × distance moved by effort.

✓ Work output = Load × distance moved by load.

◆ EFFICIENCY
η = Work output / Work input × 100%

✓ Also → η = M.A / V.R × 100%.

✓ Ideal machine → Has no energy loss.
✓ For an ideal machine → M.A = I.M.A = V.R.

title: UNIT 5 — MUST REMEMBER
notes:
◆ SIX SIMPLE MACHINES
✓ Inclined plane.
✓ Wedge.
✓ Screw.
✓ Lever.
✓ Wheel and axle.
✓ Pulley.

◆ BASIC TERMS
✓ Effort → Input force.
✓ Load → Output force.

◆ WORK
✓ Work input = Effort × effort distance.
✓ Work output = Load × load distance.

◆ MACHINE PERFORMANCE
✓ M.A = Load / Effort.
✓ V.R = Effort distance / Load distance.
✓ η = M.A / V.R × 100%.

◆ SPECIAL FORMULAS
✓ Lever → V.R = Effort arm / Load arm.
✓ Inclined plane → V.R = l/h.
✓ Wedge → V.R = l/t.
✓ Screw → IMA = πd/p.
✓ Wheel and axle → V.R = R/r.
✓ Pulley → V.R = Number of supporting rope sections.

◆ EXAM TIP
✓ Real machines → Are not 100% efficient because some input energy is lost, mainly through friction.
